questions.q: What problem does Real-Time Mode (RTM) solve, and what does it eliminate the need for?
options: Sub-second, in-the-loop latency for Declarative Pipelines, eliminating the need for a separate specialized engine like Apache Flink
It eliminates the need for Unity Catalog governance on streaming tables
It solves batch ETL cost, with no relation to latency at all
It eliminates the need to ever use Kafka as a source
questions.explain: RTM targets p99 latency in the tens-to-low-hundreds of milliseconds inside the same declarative model, removing the need to bolt on a second engine like Flink for use cases like fraud scoring or live personalization.

questions.q: What single configuration line, set at the flow level, switches a flow into Real-Time Mode?
options: spark_conf={"pipelines.trigger": "RealTime"} inside the @dp.update_flow decorator
dp.create_sink(mode="realtime")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 1)
trigger(availableNow=True) on a writeStream call
questions.explain: pipelines.trigger: "RealTime" set via spark_conf on the @dp.update_flow decorator (combined with the pipeline-level realTimeMode.enabled setting) is the switch that moves a flow onto the continuous engine.

questions.q: Once RTM is on, what does pipelines.trigger.interval actually control?
options: How often state and source offsets are checkpointed — it is not a micro-batch size, since RTM's 'batch' is long-running and processes data as it arrives
The exact micro-batch size processed on each trigger, identical to classic trigger(processingTime=...)
The maximum number of concurrent Lakebase sinks allowed
The TTL for all stateful timers across every flow in the pipeline
questions.explain: This is explicitly called out as a common point of confusion: in RTM, the interval only governs checkpoint cadence for state and offsets, not how often results are produced — the underlying batch is long-running.

questions.q: In the aircraft-tracking demo's stateful ZoneCounter processor, why does _ensure_timer only register a sweep timer if one isn't already pending?
options: Because handleInputRows fires once per row in RTM, so naively registering a timer on every row would pile up thousands of redundant timers
Because Spark only allows one timer to exist in the entire pipeline at any time
Because registering more than one timer would corrupt the MapState
Because timers are deprecated in favor of a fixed polling loop
questions.explain: Since handleInputRows is invoked per row in RTM, keeping exactly one pending timer in a ValueState (rather than registering a new one per row) avoids piling up redundant timers.

questions.q: Why does the ZoneCounter processor use a staleness-based eviction sweep instead of reacting to an explicit 'aircraft left the zone' event?
options: Because an aircraft crossing out of a zone generates no 'leave' event at all — there's nothing to react to, so a recurring TTL-based sweep evicts aircraft not seen recently
Because Kafka does not support delete events of any kind
Because explicit leave events exist but are considered too expensive to process
Because MapState cannot store timestamps, only counts
questions.explain: There's no 'leave' event to react to when an aircraft exits a zone — the sweep pattern evicts anything not seen within a short TTL and re-emits the refreshed count, letting an emptied zone clear itself automatically.
